candidates.title: The ban Mae is describing was real, and it lasted fifty years
candidates.detail: In her speech to the squad Mae says she wanted to be a footballer growing up but women were not allowed to play officially. That is not a vague complaint about sexism; it is a specific piece of English football administration. On 5 December 1921 the Football Association resolved that the game was unsuitable for females and ought not to be encouraged, and barred women's matches from grounds belonging to FA-affiliated clubs. Because almost every usable pitch in the country was affiliated, the effect was a ban. The FA did not recognise women's football again until July 1971 — fifty years later. Reviewers report that the speech names the prohibition rather than merely implying it; the exact wording should be checked, and the card must paraphrase.
candidates.moment: Before the deciding match, Mae speaks to the Richmond women's squad in the away dressing room and tells them that the game she wanted as a girl was closed to women.

candidates.title: What the ban interrupted: 53,000 people at Goodison Park
candidates.detail: The ban is usually told as a story about prudishness, but the year before it the women's game was drawing crowds the men's game would recognise. On Boxing Day 1920 more than 53,000 spectators came through the turnstiles at Goodison Park to watch Dick, Kerr Ladies beat St Helens Ladies 4-0, with thousands more locked outside; the gate receipts went to wounded and unemployed ex-servicemen. That attendance record for a women's club match in England stood for roughly a century. The FA's resolution came eleven and a half months later. This is context for Mae's speech, not something stated on screen.

candidates.title: The dates line up exactly against Mae's life
candidates.detail: The show has never given Mae's age, so this has to be done carefully. But Annette Badland was 76 at the time the episode aired, and the character is plainly of that generation — the Crown & Anchor's long-standing landlady, old enough to be the pub's matriarch. For an Englishwoman born around 1950, the FA's recognition of women's football in July 1971 arrives at about twenty-one: her entire girlhood, every year in which she might have been coached, picked, or given a pitch, falls inside the ban. That is why her line is a fact about administration rather than a lament about talent. Flagged for the reviewer: the arithmetic rests on the actress's age and the character's evident generation, not on anything the script states.

candidates.title: Why the show kills her on her best day
candidates.detail: Mae gets the thing she was denied — a dressing room, a bus, a team that wants her there, a promotion won in front of her — and then dies within the hour. There is an old idea underneath that shape. In Herodotus, Solon tells Croesus that no life can be called happy until it is finished, because fortune can still undo it; Aristotle takes the puzzle seriously in the Nicomachean Ethics, where eudaimonia is a property of a complete life rather than of a good afternoon. Badland's own reading of the ending is close to it: she has said Mae's last day was probably her best and that she was very happy. The reviewer should check that this is offered as a frame the card brings, in the app's established voice, and not as a reference the episode makes.

candidates.title: The standard account of why death is bad, run backwards
candidates.detail: The most influential modern answer to why death harms you is Thomas Nagel's deprivation account: death is bad not because being dead is unpleasant but because it takes away goods you would otherwise have had. Mae's death is built to sit awkwardly on that. She spent fifty-odd years deprived of the thing, got it, and died — so the deprivation ran before the death rather than after it, and the last hour is the one stretch of her life the account cannot call a loss. This is an interpretive frame, not a reference the episode makes; flagged as such.

candidates.title: The kid from the Pilot scores the goal that seals it
candidates.detail: Shannon is the girl with the ball Ted keeps running into around Richmond in Season 1 — they have a kickabout in the Pilot, when Ted knows almost nothing about football and she is one of the few locals not hostile to him. She turns up again at the end of Season 3 getting Trent Crimm's book signed. In Season 4 she auditions for the new women's team in Episode 3, underperforms, and is kept on anyway. Here, reportedly on her debut, she scores the goal that completes a 4-2 comeback and clinches promotion. Six years of setup paid off by a single goal. candidates.title: The card at the very end is not about Mae
candidates.detail: The episode closes on an in-memoriam card for Anthony Head, who played Rupert Mannion. Head died in June 2026, aged 72, of complications from pneumonia, according to a statement his daughters gave the BBC; Season 4 had long since finished filming. So the hour that kills off one Richmond institution ends by marking the loss of the actor who played its antagonist — a coincidence of scheduling rather than a plan. The reviewer should confirm the card's exact wording and that it is Episode 9 rather than the finale.

candidates.title: The show refuses to show you the worst moment
candidates.detail: The death is staged almost entirely by omission. Mae is seen collapsed rather than collapsing; a steward reaches her; a stadium official finds Rebecca and tells her there has been an incident involving Ms Green; Rebecca then tells Ted in a conversation the audience watches but cannot hear. Nothing on screen states that Mae has died — that came from cast interviews afterwards. Multiple recaps independently describe this structure, which makes it one of the better-sourced facts about the episode.

candidates.title: The 2.9% that has been sitting there since Season 1
candidates.detail: The ownership plot turns on the Milk sisters, the elderly minority shareholders from Season 1 who held 2.9% of AFC Richmond until Rupert bought them out. They are shareholders again in Season 4, and the episode ends with Zelda's associate Hugo Riddles sitting down with them about selling to Zelda. Rebecca holds 51% following her decision in the Season 3 finale, so Zelda cannot outvote her — the point of the scene is how close she can get. A long-dormant background detail turned into the season's pivot.

candidates.title: How hard what they just did actually is
candidates.detail: Richmond's women go up in their first season of existence. In the real English pyramid as it stands for 2026-27, exactly one club is promoted automatically from WSL2 — the champions — while the runners-up and third place fight a pre-qualifier for the right to play the thirteenth-placed WSL side in a play-off. So a first-season side winning automatic promotion means finishing first, with one guaranteed slot available. The reviewer should check whether the episode names the division or the mechanism at all; if it does not, the card must present this as real-world background and say so.

candidates.title: The same decision as last week, made the other way
candidates.detail: Episode 8 turned on Alice leaving Gemma on the pitch while Richmond were comfortably ahead, chasing a hat-trick, and Gemma's knee going. Here Gemma is back, scores, and comes off at half-time with the knee sore and the game not yet won — recaps describe her accepting the substitution rather than arguing for it. The structural point is that the episode restages last week's choice and lets both of them get it right. Recaps differ on the specifics: whether her goal is a penalty, whether she is medically cleared beforehand, and whether she asks to come off or is taken off. The card should stay at the level the sources agree on.
